Day 1
From Hotel: 8 min · 4 min → Art Institute of Chicago
1. Art Institute of Chicago
One of the world's great art museums, housed in a Beaux-Arts landmark on Michigan Avenue. The collection spans 5,000 years — Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Grant Wood's American Gothic, and Picasso's The Old Guitarist are here, alongside a world-class Impressionist collection.

1. Chicago Cultural Center
A Beaux-Arts landmark that opened in 1897 as Chicago's central library, now the city's flagship free arts venue. Preston Bradley Hall houses the world's largest Tiffany stained-glass dome — 38 feet across, built from 30,000 pieces of glass.

2. The Rookery Building
Chicago's oldest standing steel-skeleton skyscraper, completed in 1888 by Burnham and Root. The lobby is free to enter. Frank Lloyd Wright remodeled the light court in 1905, adding white marble and organic ironwork — two of America's greatest architects in the same room.

One of the world's largest fountains, built in 1927 and modeled on the Latona Fountain at Versailles at three times the scale. Water shoots 150 feet into the air hourly from mid-April through mid-October, with an evening light show at dusk.

1. Field Museum
One of the largest natural history museums on earth, built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and housing 40 million specimens across four floors. The main hall is anchored by Sue, the largest and most complete T. rex skeleton ever found, with gems, Egypt, and ancient Americas filling the wings.

The John G. Shedd Aquarium holds more than 32,000 animals across 5 million gallons of water, including beluga whales, Pacific white-sided dolphins, and a 90,000-gallon Wild Reef exhibit recreating a Philippine coral reef. Day 4
From Hotel: 18 min → Robie House
1. Robie House
Frank Lloyd Wright's masterpiece of Prairie Style, built in 1910 on the University of Chicago campus. Cantilevered eaves extend 20 feet without visible support, the Roman-brick banding reduces the house to pure horizontal geometry, and the art-glass windows dissolve the wall plane. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

One of the largest and most architecturally significant conservatories in the United States, designed by Jens Jensen in 1908 as "landscape art under glass." Eight glasshouses shelter 2,700 plant varieties — cycads over 200 years old fill the Palm House and ferns from five continents carpet the Fern Room.

Day 6
From Hotel: 25 min → Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio
1. Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio
Wright's personal home and studio from 1889 to 1909 — where he developed the Prairie Style and designed more than 150 buildings. The shingled house grew from a modest Queen Anne cottage into a sprawling laboratory with an octagonal library, a barrel-vaulted playroom, and a studio with chain-hung balcony.

8 min · 4 min → Unity Temple
2. Unity Temple
Wright's first major public commission, built in 1906 from poured concrete when the congregation could not afford stone or brick. The result was radical — a building using the material's mass as ornament, with amber art-glass skylights flooding the worship hall. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

3. Chicago Water Tower
A 154-foot Gothic Revival limestone tower built in 1869, one of the few masonry structures to survive the 1871 Great Chicago Fire. It disguises a 138-foot iron standpipe inside and has become one of Chicago's most recognized civic symbols. The City Gallery inside mounts rotating exhibitions of Chicago photography.

4. Tribune Tower
A 36-story neo-Gothic skyscraper built in 1925 following the Chicago Tribune's design competition, which drew 263 entries from 23 countries. At street level, 149 fragments from famous structures — the Colosseum, the Taj Mahal, Notre-Dame, the Berlin Wall — are embedded in the limestone base by Tribune correspondents.

Local Tastes
Chicago-Style Deep Dish Pizza
A pie unlike any other — thick buttery crust pressed up the sides of a pan, layered with cheese, fillings, then chunky crushed-tomato sauce on top. Invented at Pizzeria Uno in 1943.
Pizzeria Uno · Lou Malnati's · Giordano's
Chicago-Style Hot Dog
A Vienna Beef frank on a poppy-seed bun, dragged through the garden: yellow mustard, white onion, neon relish, a dill pickle spear, two sport peppers, tomato wedges, and celery salt. Never ketchup.
Portillo's · Gene & Jude's · Gold Coast Dogs
Chicago Italian Beef Sandwich
Thin-sliced seasoned roast beef on Turano Italian bread, dipped fully in the cooking jus and topped with giardiniera or sweet peppers. Born on the South Side in the 1930s, now a Chicago signature in every neighbourhood.
Al's Italian Beef · Portillo's · Johnnie's Beef
Garrett Popcorn – Chicago Mix
Garrett's Chicago Mix blends CaramelCrisp and CheeseCorn in the same bag — the combination that has had locals and tourists lined up on Michigan Avenue since 1949.
Garrett Popcorn Shops
Jeppson's Malört
Chicago's notoriously bitter wormwood spirit — a Swedish-origin liqueur that became a uniquely local phenomenon. The face people make on the first sip has become a Chicago rite of passage and a social-media institution.
Any bar

Worth Knowing

Chicago's Second Birth

The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 burned for two days and destroyed a third of the city. Within 20 years, the rubble had been replaced by the world's first skyscrapers — the Rookery in 1888, the Monadnock in 1891, the Reliance in 1895. The disaster, by forcing the complete reinvention of an entire city center in a single generation, accidentally created modern architecture. Every skyscraper on earth today is a direct descendant of what was built in these 16 blocks of the Loop between 1871 and 1900.

The Rookery Building holds a detail most visitors miss: in 1905, a young Frank Lloyd Wright was commissioned to renovate the light court of a building completed 17 years before he became famous. He added white marble and ornamental ironwork in his emerging Prairie style — which means the Rookery contains, in the same atrium, both the 19th-century industrial aesthetic of Burnham and Root and the 20th-century organic vision of Wright. Stand in the center and you're standing in both architectural centuries simultaneously.

Buckingham Fountain — modeled on the Latona Fountain at Versailles — was built three times larger than its source. The French original is elegant. The Chicago version is operatic. It feels like the city couldn't help itself.
